statements.text: Let’s be clear: in too many cases, the uses of AI systems are not advancing American values. They heighten discrimination and produce unequal outcomes. They threaten both individual and national security.
statements.context: Dr. Alondra Nelson Former Principal Deputy Director for Science and Society and Performing the Duties of the Director, Office of Science and Technology Policy, The White House Harold F. Linder Professor, Institute for Advanced Study Distinguished Senior Fellow, Center for American Progress ____ Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Innovation Russell Senate Office Building Washington, D.C. ___ October 24, 2023 Advanced AI presents both dangerous pitfalls and tremendous potential. A recent study put some possible numbers behind that duality, predicting that 300 million full-time jobs could be replaced by artificial intelligence. But it also suggested that instead of substituting jobs, AI could complement or create jobs, increase global GDP by seven percent, and catalyze a major productivity boom. 1 Whether these potential gains will be manifest across the domains of education, healthcare, agriculture, and equitably shared–improving the lives of the many rather than the fortunes of the few–is entirely up to us. We are, in one instance, on the precipice of transformative developments that may be enabled and accelerated by artificial intelligence: a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to prevent cancers for more people, decarbonize our economy in the face of climate change, and address seemingly intractable social problems. These same tools and systems, however, are putting those promised opportunities further out of reach by exacting a constellation of harms on us today. We need to set a better course. Let’s be clear: in too many cases, the uses of AI systems are not advancing American values. They heighten discrimination and produce unequal outcomes.
